Tlingit

Tlingit people sustain living communities in Alaska, British Columbia and Yukon. This reading path brings together a tribal political history, a collaborative Yakutat study, Teslin Tlingit Council’s Inland community accounts and Hoonah’s Glacier Bay collaboration. Language education and an editorial conversation about Raven narratives add contemporary voices and public cultural perspectives. Each account has its own community, institutional or scholarly scope; no single government, story or landscape represents every Tlingit person.

Read the sources [1] Central Council of the Tlingit and Haida Indian Tribes of Alaska [2] National Park Service / Portland State University, with Yakutat Tlingit participants [4] Teslin Tlingit Council [10] Hoonah Indian Association [9] University of Washington Press; responses by Sealaska Heritage Institute [6] Teslin Tlingit Council

These are selected starting points. The full annotated collection, source perspectives, inspection limits and remaining research questions follow below. A starting guide is not an exhaustive history or community endorsement.

01

Identity and context

Tlingit people have homelands along the northwest coast and into adjoining inland regions.

Read the sources [1] Central Council of the Tlingit and Haida Indian Tribes of Alaska

02

A path for deeper reading

Focus the next stage of research on: Lingít language, clans and houses, territorial histories and distinct contemporary governments. The sources below are selected reading paths; their authorship, dates and community scope should guide how they are used.

Read the sources [1] Central Council of the Tlingit and Haida Indian Tribes of Alaska [2] National Park Service / Portland State University, with Yakutat Tlingit participants [3] tlingitandhaida.gov

03

Reading a tribal government’s own history

The Central Council’s timeline connects its institutional development with Alaska Native Brotherhood advocacy and efforts to seek redress for land withdrawals. It begins by recognizing Tlingit and Haida as distinct peoples. Read this as the government’s own historical account, alongside local histories; the statutes and cases it names require separate inspection.

Read the sources [1] Central Council of the Tlingit and Haida Indian Tribes of Alaska

04

A Yakutat case with a stated method

Deur and colleagues’2015 study combines written records with interviews and guidance from Yakutat Tlingit representatives. Its opening pages challenge the idea that park landscapes are empty of human history and explain the report’s regional focus and limits. Yakutat relationships with coastal and glacial places should not be generalized to every Tlingit community.

Read the sources [2] National Park Service / Portland State University, with Yakutat Tlingit participants

05

Living Tlingit communities across the border

Tlingit life continues in Alaska, British Columbia and Yukon. Teslin Tlingit Council identifies its people as Inland Tlingit and describes continuing connections with coastal relatives. Its account brings together oral history, movement inland, harvest camps and contemporary artists. Teslin is one distinct community example, not a government speaking for all Tlingit people.

Read the sources [4] Teslin Tlingit Council [6] Teslin Tlingit Council

06

Clan relationships and a living government

Teslin’s public governance account describes deliberation through clan representation, with Elders advising institutions and youth contributing through their council. Its stated values connect care for land and community with personal responsibility. These descriptions show how cultural relationships enter a contemporary government; they should not be generalized into one political structure for every Tlingit community.

Read the sources [5] Teslin Tlingit Council

07

Language learning in community settings

Teslin’s language department describes classroom and video-conference classes, a resource centre, early-childhood teaching and school support. These are specific routes for learning rather than evidence of a present speaker census or programme success rate. Materials and recordings linked from the page require their own review.

Read the sources [6] Teslin Tlingit Council

08

A language curriculum built with speakers and teachers

The March 2022 working draft of Tlingit Language Proficiency Scope & Sequence offers four learning levels that are not school grades. Its introduction allows teachers and learners to adapt the sequence. Selected Level 3 goals connect conversation with kinship and community responsibilities. This is a teaching framework, not a test of whether someone belongs to a people.

Read the sources [8] Sealaska Heritage Institute with Goldbelt Heritage, University of Alaska Southeast and Juneau School District

09

Raven narratives are individual works of language art

In a February 2026 publisher conversation, Sealaska Heritage Institute explains how editors transcribe recordings, consult fluent Elders and retain storytellers’ differing sequences and styles. Its account presents Raven narratives as language art with humor as well as cultural significance. This review covers that conversation, not the book’s stories or underlying recordings. Readers should approach named tellers and particular versions rather than invent one uniform Tlingit mythology.

Read the sources [9] University of Washington Press; responses by Sealaska Heritage Institute

10

Hoonah and the work of returning home

Hoonah Indian Association describes Xunaa Shuká Hít in Glacier Bay as a home built and maintained with the National Park Service after decades of collaboration. Its page dates the dedication to 2016. The account makes continuity and reconnection visible through a specific community’s experience. Linked ceremonies and videos were not reviewed, and the page does not grant visitors access or reproduction rights.

Read the sources [10] Hoonah Indian Association

11

Salmon care is also cultural continuity

Teslin’s salmon account describes conservation restrictions alongside the loss of opportunities for young people to learn at fish camp. Its discussion of 2010 and 2018 plans connects monitoring, governance and cultural restoration, while warning that harvest limits alone cannot restore salmon. The page contains mixed-age programme information; it is not a current fishing advisory or proof of recovery.

Read the sources [7] Teslin Tlingit Council

What needs further research

  • Review additional Tlingit-authored histories and language resources from distinct coastal and inland communities.
  • Read further Yakutat chapters and community-directed studies before discussing particular clan histories, places or resource practices.
  • Further Tlingit-authored histories from additional coastal and inland communities; these Teslin, Hoonah and Yakutat examples are not comprehensive.
  • Read appropriately public oral-literature volumes and permissions separately; this review covers an editorial conversation, not underlying narratives or recordings.
  • Assess language programmes through dated community-released results before reporting present fluency, attendance or outcomes.
  • Read additional Yakutat chapters and locally authorized sources before expanding specific clan histories, places or practices.
  • Contemporary salmon status, adopted rules and monitoring results need separate dated evidence; mixed-age web text is not a current advisory.
